newsitem.title: LEBANON: FOCUS - Beirut's Byblos Bank plans $50 mln Euronote.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Beirut's Byblos Bank plans $50 mln Euronote.

text.p: Fast-growing Byblos Bank said on Friday it planned a $50 million Euronote on September 9, making it Lebanon's second commercial bank to raise money on the international debt market.

Byblos, which last year raised $11.6 million on the international equity market in a heavily-oversubscribed private share placement, is one of Lebanon's most dynamic banks, a trailblazer in the mortgage, credit card and personal loans business.
Its total assets and customer deposits have nearly trebled since 1993 to more than $1 billion each.
Proceeds from the Euronote will be used to increase its personal loans business, deputy general manager Gerard Charvet told Reuters.

SBC Warburg and Beirut finance house Lebanon Invest SAL, who are managing the issue, said it would be priced around 300 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasury notes and would be listed on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange.
Road shows will be held in Geneva on September 4 and in London on September 5.
Executives at Byblos and Lebanon Invest said the currently gloomy political climate in the Middle East was not apparently discouraging potential investors.
"The first reaction we have so far is favourable in Europe," Charvet said. "There is demand in Europe for this kind of paper."
Bernard Mouchabahani, corporate finance manager at Lebanon Invest, said: "The selling has been going very well. We think the notes are priced very well. It's attracting a lot of interest."
Bassam Yammine, a corporate finance and currency executive at Lebanon Invest, said European investors had developed an appetite for Lebanese debt.

"Fixed income is being taken very quickly," he said. "Two years ago everyone wanted equity. Today I don't get a refusal on debt, with the Eurobond yielding over nine percent compared with deposit interest at six or seven percent."

A trailblazing $60 million Eurobond issue in June by Credit Libanais, which was managed by Merrill Lynch International, showed the interest of international markets in Lebanese paper despite the clouding of Middle East peace prospects this year.
Credit Libanais' issue was closely watched by other Beirut banks interested in going into the international debt market.
Their interest is largely due to the lack of medium and long-term money in Lebanon where the average customer deposit is only a few weeks.
Byblos has 27 branches in Lebanon and an offshore unit in Cyprus.

The bank's total assets were $1.19 billion at the end of June, compared with $430 million in 1993, making it Lebanon's sixth largest bank in terms of total assets. Deposits were $1.01 billion compared with $377 million in 1993.
